about: Brixton market in the morning, then a walk up Brixton Hill and round Brockwell Park.

cards.line: Did you know, Brixton's Electric Avenue was the first market street lit by electricity?
cards.fact: Electric Avenue in Brixton was the first market street to be lit by electricity. Eddy Grant's 1982 hit song Electric Avenue is named after it.

cards.line: Did you know, Brixton Village market was nearly replaced by a 10-storey tower in 2008?
cards.fact: In 2008 new owners planned to replace the 1937 Granville Arcade with a 10-storey tower. Traders and locals fought it off, and it was listed in 2010.

cards.line: Did you know, Laurel and Hardy once played a Brixton music hall that's now housing?
cards.fact: The Empress opened in 1898 and later hosted Marie Lloyd, Vera Lynn and Laurel and Hardy. It became a cinema, then bingo, and was knocked down in 1992.

cards.line: Did you know, Brixton is named after a Saxon lord's stone?
cards.fact: Brixton means Brixi's stone. Brixi, a Saxon lord, is thought to have set up a stone at the top of what's now Brixton Hill, to mark where the local court met.

cards.line: Did you know, about 150,000 people filled Brockwell Park for a Rock Against Racism concert in 1978?
cards.fact: In 1978 about 150,000 came to a Rock Against Racism carnival in Brockwell Park, headlined by the singer Elvis Costello. Some watched from trees.

about: Herne Hill up Railton Road into Brixton, lunch in Wandsworth, then Battersea Power Station.

cards.line: Did you know, two Black Panthers squatted on Railton Road in 1972 and fought off eviction?
cards.fact: In 1972 two women from the British Black Panthers took over a flat above a Railton Road launderette, then opened number 121, squatted until 1999.

cards.line: Did you know, police stopped almost 1,000 people in Brixton in 5 days just before the 1981 riot?
cards.fact: In April 1981 plain-clothes police were sent into Brixton. In 5 days they stopped almost 1,000 people, mostly young black men. Rioting followed.

cards.line: Did you know, St Matthew's church in Brixton was one of the churches built to celebrate victory at Waterloo?
cards.fact: St Matthew's, finished in 1824 on land taken from Rush Common, was one of the Waterloo churches, built to celebrate Britain's win at Waterloo.
cards.source: Wikipedia: St Matthew's Church, Brixton; Brixton

cards.line: Did you know, Wandsworth and the River Wandle are named after the same man?
cards.fact: Wandsworth means the enclosure of a man called Waendel. The River Wandle, which joins the Thames there, is named after him too.

cards.line: Did you know, the machines that dug the tube tunnels to Battersea were called Helen and Amy?
cards.fact: Local schoolchildren named the two machines that dug the Northern line tunnels to Battersea. They chose Helen and Amy, after the astronaut Helen Sharman and the pilot Amy Johnson.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Northern line extension to Battersea

about: Across Clapham Common to the tube, lunch near Waterloo, back over Waterloo Bridge.

cards.line: Did you know, two mounds on Clapham Common are left over from a Second World War gun site?
cards.fact: In the Second World War Clapham Common had a heavy anti-aircraft gun site. Two mounds on the Battersea Rise side are left from its storage bunkers.

cards.line: Did you know, Jamaican arrivals in 1948 were housed in an air-raid shelter under Clapham South station?
cards.fact: In 1948 a ship brought 492 people from Jamaica to fill London's jobs. With nowhere else to house them, many slept in the shelter under Clapham South.

cards.line: Did you know, MI6's secret headquarters from 1964 was an office block on Westminster Bridge Road?
cards.fact: From 1964 MI6 was based at Century House on Westminster Bridge Road. Its address was officially secret, yet a paper said every taxi driver knew it.

cards.line: Did you know, Lambeth means a landing place for lambs?
cards.fact: Lambeth was first written Lambehitha in 1062, meaning a landing place for lambs. It was a riverside harbour where lambs were shipped in or out.

cards.line: Did you know, a writer was assassinated with an umbrella on Waterloo Bridge?
cards.fact: In 1978 the Bulgarian writer Georgi Markov was waiting for a bus on Waterloo Bridge when a man used an umbrella to put a tiny pellet of poison into his leg.
cards.source: Wikipedia: Georgi Markov; Wikipedia: Waterloo Bridge

about: After work, from the Oval through Vauxhall and along the river to the South Bank.

cards.line: Did you know, the Oval cricket ground was a cabbage patch until 1845?
cards.fact: In 1844 the Oval was a Duchy of Cornwall cabbage patch. In spring 1845, 10,000 turfs from Tooting Common were laid, and cricket began that May.

cards.line: Did you know, in the Second World War the Oval was made a camp for enemy parachutists?
cards.fact: In the Second World War the Oval cricket ground became a prisoner-of-war camp for enemy parachutists. None ever landed, so it was never used.

cards.line: Did you know, a Vauxhall homeless shelter opened in an old Marmite factory?
cards.fact: In 1973 the homeless charity St Mungo's opened a hostel for up to 200 people in a disused Marmite factory in Vauxhall.

cards.line: Did you know, Vauxhall is named after King John's mercenary chief?
cards.fact: Vauxhall is named after Falkes de Breauté, who led King John's hired soldiers. He had a big house here, known as Faulke's Hall, and over time the name became Vauxhall.

cards.line: Did you know, the Royal Festival Hall stands where a woman ran a factory making artificial stone for royal palaces?
cards.fact: Where the Royal Festival Hall stands, Eleanor Coade made a weatherproof artificial stone from 1769 to 1821. Kings used it in their palaces.
